sections.overview: Montastraea cavernosa is a widespread reef-building stony coral of the tropical Atlantic and Caribbean.
sections.identification: Its colonies form rounded masses, domes or pillars, sometimes flattened at depth. The large, star-shaped polyps are about 6–12 mm across and vary from brown or green to grey or violet.
sections.habitat: It occupies many reef settings from shallow water to at least 100 m; abundance is often greatest at intermediate depths, and it tolerates some turbid conditions.
sections.diet: At night, extended polyps capture plankton and other small particles with their tentacles; symbiotic algae also contribute energy.
sections.behavior: The polyps usually retract during the day and extend at night to feed.
sections.reproduction: It releases eggs and sperm into the water during synchronized spawning; colonies have separate sexes, unlike many broadcast-spawning corals.
sections.ecology: The coral’s tissues host symbiotic algae. Heat stress can disrupt this partnership, causing bleaching and weakening the colony.
sections.conservation: The IUCN assessment lists it as Least Concern, but that global assessment dates to 2008 and notes reef-habitat loss and climate-related threats.
